items.headline: New nonprescription eye drop approved for redness relief
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new nonprescription eye drop to relieve eye redness. It is available without a prescription for over-the-counter use.
items.why_it_matters: You can now buy this eye drop without a prescription to help reduce redness in your eyes.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved Brytly, a nonprescription eye drop containing apraclonidine at 0.125%, for relief of eye redness due to minor irritations. It is the first nonprescription eye drop with apraclonidine and is approved for use in adults and children 12 years of age and older. The product should not be used more than two times per day. Consumers are advised to remove contact lenses before use and wait at least 10 minutes before reinserting them. Use should be stopped and a doctor consulted if eye pain, vision changes, continued redness, or irritation occurs, or if symptoms persist beyond three days.
key_findings: Approved for over-the-counter use in adults and children 12 years and older.

items.headline: Cognitive therapy may prevent chronic back pain
items.summary: A clinical trial found that cognitive functional therapy reduced the risk of acute low back pain becoming long-term disability. The study compared this therapy to usual care in patients with back pain lasting less than three months.
items.why_it_matters: If you have recent back pain, early cognitive therapy may help prevent it from becoming long-lasting.

The study will compare CFT to usual care in patients with back pain lasting less than three months. The primary outcome is average low back pain-related disability over 12 months. The trial plans to enroll 461 participants and will assess cost-effectiveness and long-term effects over 3 years.

items.headline: New drug recommended for approval in Europe for pancreatic cancer
items.summary: European regulators have recommended approval for a new pancreatic cancer drug following FDA approval. The recommendation marks a key step toward wider availability in Europe.
items.why_it_matters: This could mean faster access to a new treatment option for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer in Europe.

detail.summary: European regulators have recommended approval for Rasonque (daraxonrasib) for adult patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or are not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy. The recommendation follows FDA approval and is based on a phase 3 trial comparing daraxonrasib to chemotherapy in previously treated patients. In the trial, daraxonrasib significantly improved overall survival and progression-free survival compared to chemotherapy in patients with RAS G12 mutations and in the overall population. Adverse events were common but less frequent at grade 3 or higher than with chemotherapy.
key_findings: Median overall survival was 13.2 months with daraxonrasib and 6.6 months with chemotherapy in the RAS G12 population (hazard ratio 0.40, P<0.001)
Median overall survival was 13.2 months with daraxonrasib and 6.7 months with chemotherapy in the overall population (hazard ratio 0.40, P<0.001)
Median progression-free survival was 7.3 months with daraxonrasib and 3.5 months with chemotherapy in the RAS G12 population (hazard ratio 0.45, P<0.001)
Median progression-free survival was 7.2 months with daraxonrasib and 3.6 months with chemotherapy in the overall population (hazard ratio 0.49, P<0.001)
Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 61.8% of patients on daraxonrasib and 69.6% on chemotherapy

study.primary_endpoint: overall survival and progression-free survival in the subpopulation of patients with RAS G12 mutations

detail.regulatory_status: European regulators have recommended approval; FDA has already approved
caveats: Adverse events occurred in all patients on daraxonrasib, with grade 3 or higher events in 61.8%

The drug is not approved for first-line use

items.headline: FDA Approves First Treatment for Advanced Bladder Cancer
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new treatment for adults with certain types of bladder cancer that no longer respond to BCG therapy. This approval marks the first option for this specific group of patients.
items.why_it_matters: People with advanced bladder cancer that doesn’t respond to standard therapy now have a new treatment option.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved Anktiva in combination with BCG for adults with high-grade papillary-only bladder cancer that has not responded to BCG therapy. This approval is based on evidence from a trial (NCT03022825) that evaluated the treatment in patients with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. The trial showed that 58.2% of patients remained disease-free at 12 months, and 38.2% at 36 months. The FDA used data from patients with carcinoma in situ (CIS) to support approval for this specific group due to clinical and biological similarities.

38.2% disease-free survival at 36 months (95% CI: 25.6, 50.6)
83.1% progression-free survival at 36 months (95% CI: 69.5, 91.0)
92.2% cystectomy avoidance at 12 months (95% CI: 83.4, 96.4)
81.8% cystectomy avoidance at 36 months (95% CI: 68.1, 90.1)

study.primary_endpoint: disease-free survival at 12 months

detail.regulatory_status: FDA approved for BCG-unresponsive high-grade papillary-only nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer
caveats: The approval is based on extrapolation from data in patients with CIS, not a direct trial in papillary-only disease

Delaying surgery may allow cancer to spread, which can be fatal

items.headline: New treatment approved for aggressive bladder cancer
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new treatment for adults with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. It is used in combination with BCG to help prevent cancer progression.
items.why_it_matters: If you or a loved one has this type of bladder cancer, this approval offers a new treatment option after BCG failure.

detail.summary: The FDA approved nogapendekin alfa inbakicept-pmln in combination with BCG for adults with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. This includes patients with high-grade papillary-only tumors, expanding the prior indication that was limited to those with carcinoma in situ (CIS) with or without papillary tumors. Efficacy was demonstrated in a single-arm trial of 77 patients with BCG-unresponsive, high-risk NMIBC and CIS, where 62% achieved a complete response. The treatment was given as intravesical instillation once a week for 6 weeks as induction, followed by maintenance therapy. The approval is based on extrapolation from prior evidence in CIS patients, due to overlapping clinical and pathological features with papillary disease.
key_findings: Complete response rate was 62% (95% CI: 51, 73) in patients with BCG-unresponsive NMIBC and CIS.
58% of patients with complete response had a duration of response of at least 12 months.
40% of patients with complete response had a duration of response of at least 24 months.
The indication was expanded to include high-grade papillary-only tumors based on shared clinical and non-clinical features with CIS.
The maximum treatment duration is 37 months, with maintenance doses at months 4, 7, 10, 13, 19, and optionally at months 25, 31, 37.

study.primary_endpoint: complete response (CR) as determined by cystoscopy, urine cytology, and biopsy

detail.regulatory_status: FDA approved on October 14, 2026, for BCG-unresponsive NMIBC with CIS with or without papillary tumors, now expanded to include high-grade papillary-only tumors
caveats: The approval for papillary-only tumors is based on extrapolation from CIS data, not direct evidence in that subgroup.
The most common adverse reactions occurred in ≥15% of patients, including increased creatinine, dysuria, hematuria, and urinary tract infection.
The label includes a warning that delaying cystectomy can lead to metastatic bladder cancer, which can be lethal.
detail.next_steps: FDA is working toward finalizing the Guidance for Industry on BCG-unresponsive NMIBC to address the approach of extrapolating efficacy across histologic subtypes.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Adults with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer, including those with high-grade papillary-only tumors or carcinoma in situ with or without papillary tumors

items.headline: Core exercises improved jumping and balance in teen soccer players
items.summary: An 8-week core exercise program improved jumping and balance in recreational soccer players aged 14 to 16. The study found measurable gains in performance without injury.
items.why_it_matters: Teen athletes can boost performance and stability with just 8 weeks of simple core training.

detail.summary: Thirty-six recreational male soccer players aged 14 to 16 were randomly assigned to an experimental group that performed a structured core exercise program twice a week in addition to regular soccer training, or a control group that continued only regular soccer training. The program included a 3-minute dynamic activation, 15 minutes of core exercises, and a 2-minute cool-down. Outcomes measured were standing long jump distance, vertical jump height (squat jump), and static balance (Flamingo Balance Test) before and after the 8-week period.

items.headline: New antibody therapy mimics clotting factor for hemophilia A
items.summary: A bispecific antibody has been developed to mimic factor VIII, treating hemophilia A. It offers a new treatment option for patients with this inherited bleeding disorder.
items.why_it_matters: People with hemophilia A may now have a new treatment that reduces bleeding risk without frequent infusions.

detail.summary: A bispecific antibody called emicizumab was tested in patients with hemophilia A, both with and without factor VIII inhibitors. In a phase 3 trial, it was given as prophylaxis via subcutaneous injection once weekly or every two weeks. Compared to no prophylaxis, emicizumab reduced the annualized bleeding rate by 96% to 97%. Long-term data from pooled studies showed sustained low bleeding rates, with 82.4% of patients having no treated bleeds during weeks 121 to 144.
key_findings: Annualized bleeding rate was 1.5 events per year in the weekly dosing group (95% CI, 0.9 to 2.5)

Annualized bleeding rate was 38.2 events per year in the no prophylaxis group (95% CI, 22.9 to 63.8)

No new safety concerns were identified after 970.3 patient-years of exposure

items.headline: Cold-stored platelets work as well as room-temp ones in heart surgery
items.summary: In patients bleeding during heart surgery, platelets stored cold for up to 21 days were as safe and effective as those stored at room temperature for 5 to 7 days.
items.why_it_matters: This could extend platelet supply and reduce waste, improving availability for critical surgeries.

detail.summary: In patients bleeding during heart surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass, platelets stored cold (1-6 °C) for up to 21 days were tested against room-temperature platelets (20-24 °C) stored for up to 7 days. The trial found that cold-stored platelets were noninferior to room-temperature platelets in controlling bleeding. There was no significant difference in 24-hour chest tube output or major adverse events, except for higher reexploration rates in the cold-stored group. The results suggest cold-stored platelets could reduce waste and improve availability.
key_findings: Cold-stored platelets were noninferior to room-temperature platelets for hemostatic efficacy (posterior probability >99.9% for all storage durations)
Mean difference in hemostatic efficacy score: 0.09 (95% credible interval, -0.06 to 0.23)
Median 24-hour chest tube output: 8.9 mL/kg for cold-stored vs. 8.4 mL/kg for room-temperature (difference in medians: 0.4 mL/kg, 95% CI -1.0 to 1.5)
No significant differences in thrombotic events, acute respiratory distress syndrome, kidney failure, septic shock, or mortality
Higher reexploration rates in the cold-stored platelet group

study.design: phase 3, multicenter, randomized, partially blinded, adaptive, noninferiority, storage duration-ranging trial
study.participants: 1000 patients who underwent platelet transfusion; 989 included in primary analysis (650 cold-stored, 339 room-temperature)
study.comparator: Room-temperature platelets stored for up to 7 days
study.primary_endpoint: Hemostatic efficacy score (1 to 5, higher values indicate greater bleeding)

caveats: Higher reexploration rates in the cold-stored platelet group

items.summary: A new drug significantly reduced cholestatic pruritus in patients with rare liver diseases, including biliary atresia. The results were compared to placebo in a late-stage trial.

detail.summary: In a late-stage trial, Livmarli significantly reduced cholestatic pruritus in patients with rare liver diseases, including biliary atresia. The study compared the drug to placebo in a randomized, double-blind, phase 3 trial. Participants included patients with cholestatic pruritus due to rare liver diseases such as Alagille syndrome, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and biliary atresia.

items.headline: New drug shows promise in slowing lung scarring
items.summary: A Phase 3 trial showed that a new drug significantly slowed the progression of lung fibrosis. Results demonstrated a meaningful improvement in lung function compared to placebo.
items.why_it_matters: People with progressive lung scarring may now have a new treatment option to help preserve breathing function.

detail.summary: A Phase 3 trial tested admilparant in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). The 60 mg dose significantly slowed lung function decline compared to placebo, while the 120 mg dose failed. Results showed a meaningful improvement in lung function and delayed disease progression. The drug was well tolerated, with no deaths reported as first progression events in the trial.
key_findings: The 60 mg dose of admilparant reduced the rate of decline in percent predicted FVC by 1.4% over 26 weeks in IPF patients compared to placebo.
In PPF patients, the 60 mg dose reduced decline by 3.2% compared to placebo.
Time to disease progression was delayed in both IPF and PPF cohorts with the 60 mg dose (hazard ratio 0.54 for IPF, 0.41 for PPF).
No deaths were reported as the first event of disease progression in either cohort.
Treatment discontinuations due to adverse events were lower with the 60 mg dose (0%) than with placebo (17.1%) in PPF patients.

caveats: The higher 120 mg dose failed, indicating a narrow therapeutic window.
No mortality benefit was observed, and the trial used surrogate endpoints.
Adverse events were not fully detailed in the source, though earlier trials noted diarrhea and blood pressure changes.
detail.next_steps: Further evaluation and potential regulatory review based on Phase 3 results.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) or progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF).

items.headline: New wearable tracks blood sugar and ketones continuously
items.summary: The Libre Duo 10 Day system is approved for people aged 2 and older with diabetes. It provides continuous monitoring of both glucose and ketone levels.
items.why_it_matters: People with diabetes can now track two key health markers in real time with a single wearable device.

detail.intervention: Libre Duo 10 Day Continuous Dual Glucose Ketone Monitoring System
detail.summary: The Libre Duo 10 Day system is a wearable device approved by the FDA for continuous monitoring of both blood glucose and ketone levels in people aged 2 years and older with diabetes. It measures these levels every minute under the skin and sends data wirelessly to a smartphone. The device can alert users when ketone levels reach a concerning threshold, potentially helping prevent diabetic ketoacidosis. The FDA authorization was based on data from six clinical studies involving over 600 participants. The system was shown to accurately track clinically meaningful changes in ketone levels across its 10-day wear period.
key_findings: The device continuously monitors both glucose and ketone levels every minute.
It accurately tracked clinically meaningful differences in ketone levels across a 10-day wear period.
It identified elevated ketone levels before the onset of diabetic ketoacidosis.
It provides real-time data and automatic alerts for rising ketone levels.
It is the first wearable device in the U.S. to continuously monitor both glucose and ketones.

items.headline: New drug approved for stubborn herpes sores in immune-compromised adults
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new drug for adults with weakened immune systems who have not responded to other treatments for herpes simplex virus skin and mucosal lesions. It is intended for patients who continue to have sores despite prior therapy.
items.why_it_matters: If you or someone you know has persistent herpes sores and a weakened immune system, this approval offers a new treatment option.

The approval is based on a phase 3 trial in 101 immunocompromised adults with refractory HSV infections. By day 28, 63% of patients treated with pritelivir had all lesions healed, compared to 34% in the comparator group. The most common side effect was headache. The drug is intended for patients with no other effective treatment options.

items.headline: New drug approved for rare blood disorder causing excess red blood cells
items.summary: The FDA has approved rusfertide for adults with polycythemia vera, a rare blood disorder that causes the body to produce too many red blood cells. This is the first drug of its kind approved for this condition.
items.why_it_matters: People with polycythemia vera should talk to their doctor about this new treatment option.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved rusfertide (Mimrylo) for adults with polycythemia vera who require frequent phlebotomies despite standard therapy. In the VERIFY trial, a phase 3 study, 293 adults with polycythemia vera were randomized 1:1 to receive rusfertide or placebo for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who did not require phlebotomy between weeks 20 and 32. Rusfertide significantly reduced the need for phlebotomy compared to placebo.
key_findings: 76.9% of patients on rusfertide required no phlebotomies during weeks 20–32, compared to 32.9% on placebo.
Rusfertide was administered subcutaneously once weekly, starting at 19 mg.
Common adverse reactions included injection site reactions and anemia.
Rusfertide is the first hepcidin mimetic approved for polycythemia vera.

items.summary: The FDA has approved a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy for adults and children with Stage III colon cancer that has a specific genetic defect. This treatment is intended to reduce the risk of cancer returning after surgery.
items.why_it_matters: If you or a loved one has this type of colon cancer, ask your doctor if this new option is right for you.

items.headline: FDA approves first oral drug for adult dermatomyositis
items.summary: The FDA has approved brepocitinib tablets for treating dermatomyositis in adults. This is the first oral medication approved specifically for this condition.
items.why_it_matters: People with dermatomyositis now have a new, convenient treatment option approved by the FDA.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved brepocitinib (Lisraya) tablets for the treatment of dermatomyositis in adults. The approval is based on a phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 241 adults with dermatomyositis. Participants receiving 30 mg of brepocitinib once daily showed significantly greater improvement in disease activity compared to placebo, as measured by the Total Improvement Score at week 52. The drug also led to improvements in skin disease activity, physical function, and reduced corticosteroid use. Serious infections, increased mortality risk, malignancies, major cardiovascular events, and blood clots are noted as boxed warnings.
key_findings: Mean Total Improvement Score at week 52 was 46.5 in the 30 mg brepocitinib group vs. 31.2 in the placebo group.
The difference in TIS between brepocitinib 30 mg and placebo was 15.3 (95% CI, 6.7 to 24.0; P<0.001).
Brepocitinib 30 mg was superior to placebo across all nine key secondary endpoints, including skin disease activity and glucocorticoid tapering.
Serious infections occurred in 10% of the brepocitinib 30 mg group vs. 1% in the placebo group.
Discontinuation due to adverse reactions occurred in 6% of brepocitinib 30 mg users vs. 11% in the placebo group.

items.headline: New drug approved for advanced pancreatic cancer
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new targeted therapy for metastatic pancreatic cancer. It is the first of its kind to treat the most common form of this aggressive disease.
items.why_it_matters: Patients with advanced pancreatic cancer now have a new treatment option approved ahead of schedule.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved Rasonque (daraxonrasib) for adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or are not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy. In a phase 3 trial involving 500 adults with previously treated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, Rasonque improved median overall survival to 13.2 months compared to 6.7 months with chemotherapy. The drug targets multiple forms of the RAS protein, which drives tumor growth in most cases of this cancer. The approval was granted 6.5 months ahead of the user fee deadline, reflecting the FDA’s accelerated review process. Common side effects include rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, decreased appetite, and hemorrhage.

Median progression-free survival was 7.2 months with Rasonque vs. 3.6 months with chemotherapy.

Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 61.8% of patients on Rasonque and 69.6% on chemotherapy.

items.headline: First gene therapy approved for children with Sanfilippo syndrome
items.summary: The FDA has approved the first gene therapy for children with Sanfilippo syndrome type A, a rare inherited metabolic disorder. This treatment offers a new option for a condition that previously had no approved therapy.
items.why_it_matters: Families of children with this rare disease now have access to a treatment that may slow progression and improve quality of life.

The therapy uses an AAV9 vector to deliver a functional SGSH gene, enabling production of the missing sulfamidase enzyme. In a clinical study, treated children maintained or improved cognitive function compared to an untreated historical control cohort. The treatment is administered in a healthcare setting with pre- and post-infusion corticosteroids. Safety concerns include liver enzyme increases, thrombotic microangiopathy, and potential long-term risk of tumor development.

items.headline: New treatment approved for advanced breast cancer
items.summary: The FDA has granted accelerated approval to a new treatment for adult patients with advanced breast cancer. This expands available options for patients who need new therapies.
items.why_it_matters: Patients with advanced breast cancer now have access to a newly approved treatment option.

detail.summary: The FDA has granted accelerated approval to Etcamah (camizestrant) in combination with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for adult patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer who have an ESR1 mutation detected during treatment with an aromatase inhibitor and a CDK4/6 inhibitor. The approval was based on a clinical trial comparing switching to camizestrant plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor versus continuing an aromatase inhibitor plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor in patients with ESR1 mutations detected in blood. The trial showed a median progression-free survival of 16 months in the camizestrant group versus 9.2 months in the aromatase inhibitor group. The FDA requires confirmatory trials to verify clinical benefit.

items.summary: The FDA has approved a new combination therapy for adults with advanced HER2-positive breast cancer. It is used after initial treatment to help maintain control of the disease.
items.why_it_matters: This approval offers a new maintenance option for patients with advanced HER2-positive breast cancer, potentially extending time without disease progression.

items.headline: FDA approves first drug for Alexander disease
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new injection for treating Alexander disease in both children and adults. This is the first approved treatment for this rare neurological condition.
items.why_it_matters: People with Alexander disease now have their first approved treatment option, offering new hope for managing the disease.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved Zanvastro (zilganersen) injection for the treatment of Alexander disease in pediatric and adult patients. The drug was evaluated in a multicenter, randomized, controlled clinical study involving 49 patients aged 2 years and older, with an open-label substudy in 4 patients under 2 years. In patients aged 5 years and older, Zanvastro showed significantly better walking speed at 61 weeks compared to no treatment. In children aged 2 to 4 years, motor skills improved with treatment while declining in the control group. The approval extends to patients from infancy through adulthood based on pharmacokinetic modeling and safety data.

In children aged 2 to 4 years, motor skills (standing, walking, running, jumping) improved with Zanvastro while declining in the control group.
Pharmacokinetic modeling showed drug levels in patients under 2 years were expected to be similar to those in older children at the same dose.
Safety data from 4 patients under 2 years supported the extension of the indication to this age group.
Zanvastro is the first FDA-approved treatment for Alexander disease and the first therapy targeting the underlying GFAP protein buildup.

items.headline: First heart valve designed to grow with children gets FDA approval

items.why_it_matters: Children with this condition may avoid repeated surgeries as the valve can adapt to their growth.

detail.summary: The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve was approved by the FDA for pediatric patients with congenital pulmonary valve disease. The device uses synthetic polymeric leaflets instead of animal tissue and can be expanded from 13 mm to 22 mm in diameter using a balloon catheter. In a clinical study of 62 patients, the valve showed acceptable hemodynamic performance at six months, with no more than mild leakage and no deaths or major complications. Two patients showed early signs of valve deterioration due to growth, but both were successfully expanded non-surgically.

items.summary: People were more likely to quit smoking using nicotine vapes compared to traditional nicotine replacement therapies like patches or gum. The updated Cochrane review found a significant difference in success rates.
items.why_it_matters: If you're trying to quit smoking, nicotine vapes may offer a more effective option than gum or patches.
